newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-UK stocks claw back losses after early dip.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-UK stocks claw back losses after early dip.

text.p: A feared major sell-off of UK stocks failed to materialise on Monday, Britain's leading share index ending just 0.6 percent lower as investors took heart from an initial rise on Wall Street.
Worries over an aftershock following Friday's 22 billion pound ($35.4 billion) share writeoff proved overblown and buyers emerged following four days of decline, market sources said.

The FTSE 100 closed down 30.8 points, or 0.63 percent, at 4,835.0. The index of leading London stocks had fallen as low as 4,779.3 early on but clawed back much of the losses, Wall Street's higher opening helping to soothe nerves.
Both London and New York recorded their biggest one-day drop since 1987 on Friday and the FTSE 100 posted its largest percentage loss since 1992.

"My belief is that this is an aberration and if institutional investors take advantage of the correction to get back in, both U.S. and domestic investors, we may see a strong end to the week," said Savvas Savouri, a strategist at Credit Lyonnais Laing.
Many strategists and traders said the 2.5 percent FTSE selloff on Friday was more a correction to this year's record run rather than the start of a bear market.
Expectations for UK interest rates to stay on hold for the time being, after four hikes in four months, and high cash levels among institutions were prime reasons.

But another sharp drop in the Dow industrials or fears of monetary tightening in the U.S. or continental Europe, would rattle London investors, and some warned that as much as a 10 percent correction would ensue.

London's blue-chip index had gained 24 percent this year to its all-time best of 5,095.3 hit on August 7. Since then, it has lost 6.2 percent and Friday's drop was the largest percentage fall in five years.
The weekend may also have proved more soothing than worrying, sources said, as investors had a couple of extra days to ponder the sell-off and think about the market's fundamentals.
"We've got a 4,800 year-end target and we don't expect it to move a lot from here," said Ian Scott, UK equity strategist at Lehman Brothers.
A sharp recovery in the broader market in the last two weeks -- the second-line FTSE 250 actually ended higher on Friday -- also alleviated fears of a full-blown bear market, market sources said.
The FTSE 250 finished 0.74 percent, or 34.6 points lower at 4,663.6 on Monday after hitting a five-month high of 4,712.9 on Friday.

Sterling's retreat against the German mark after the Bank of England signalled early this month that interest rates may stay on hold, has boosted the fortunes of the second-tier industrial companies with a large percentage of overseas earnings.
Those companies' profits were hit by sterling's rise as their earnings dwindle when converted from the local currency. ($ = 0.620 British Pounds)
